notes: Unduly lenient GMC sanction reference; statutory test and remittal outcome are clear.

enrichment.short_title: CRHP reference: unduly lenient sanction for GP-patient sexual misconduct

statutes_considered.title: National Health Service and Health Care Professionals Act 2002

key_facts: Dr Leeper admitted serious professional misconduct after a prolonged sexual relationship with a vulnerable depressed patient, Mrs A.
The GMC Professional Conduct Committee imposed registration conditions for two years rather than suspension or erasure.
The Council for the Regulation of Healthcare Professionals referred the case as unduly lenient under section 29 of the 2002 Act.
Strong mitigation included about 250 testimonials, psychiatric evidence and the doctor's remorse, but the misconduct was repeated after the patient tried to end the affair.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court reference under section 29 of the 2002 Act treated as an appeal against an unduly lenient GMC disciplinary decision.
enrichment.outcome: The PCC direction was unduly lenient and suspension was the minimum appropriate sanction, but the court remitted with a direction that no further suspension be imposed because Dr Leeper had recently returned to practice and public interest favoured retention of his services.
enrichment.ratio: On a section 29 reference the court applies the statutory test of undue lenience, not the ordinary CPR 'wrong decision' appeal standard; where a penalty was unduly lenient the court may substitute or remit, and double jeopardy does not apply to such references.
legal_issues: Whether the court on a section 29 reference applies an unduly lenient or ordinary appeal test
Whether a finding of serious professional misconduct with no penalty falls within section 29(4)(a) or (b)
Whether conditions were an adequate sanction for sexual misconduct with a vulnerable patient
Whether further suspension remained in the public interest
linked_authorities: Council for the Regulation of Healthcare Professionals v The Nursing and Midwifery Council [2004] EWHC 585 (Admin)
Council for the Regulation of Healthcare Professionals v General Medical Council [2004] EWHC 944 (Admin)

notes: Interlocutory distributorship set-off and arbitration issues; Morison J's revised judgment is detailed and clear.

enrichment.short_title: Benford v Lopecan: transaction set-off and arbitration in distributorship dispute
key_facts: Spanish distributor Lopecan disputed territory under a distributorship agreement with Benford group suppliers and claimed breach by appointment of rival distributors in Cordoba and other provinces.
Benford claimed the price of trucks sold under invoice terms including retention of title and a no set-off clause, while Lopecan counterclaimed for substantial unliquidated damages.
Lopecan argued the counterclaim was a transaction set-off closely connected with the price claim and that the distributorship agreement contained an ICC arbitration clause.
The claimants contended clause 18.3 bifurcated claims for price from broader distributorship disputes and that invoice terms governed individual sales.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory applications in the Commercial Court for summary judgment, stay of counterclaim pending arbitration, and stay of execution.
enrichment.outcome: Defendants had an arguable transaction set-off defence to the price claim and arguable issues on retention of title; no stay of the counterclaim was ordered because the 'action' under clause 18.3 included claim and partial set-off counterclaim; a stay of execution would have been granted if judgment had been entered.
enrichment.ratio: A counterclaim for damages arising from breach of the umbrella distributorship agreement may operate as a transaction set-off against a claim for the price of goods sold under that relationship; an arbitration clause referring to an 'action' arising from an order can sensibly cover both claim and transactional set-off counterclaim so as to avoid bifurcated one-stop litigation.
legal_issues: Whether Lopecan had a real prospect of defending the price and delivery-up claims
Whether the counterclaim was a transaction or independent set-off
Whether invoice terms or distributorship agreement terms governed the sales
Whether the counterclaim should be stayed under the ICC arbitration clause

Dole Dried Fruit and Nut Co v Trustin Kerwood Ltd [1990] 2 Lloyd's Rep 309
Bim Kemi AB v Blackburn Chemicals Ltd [2001] 2 Lloyd's Rep 93

notes: Restrictive covenant trial judgment; enforceability analysis and injunction outcome are comprehensive.

enrichment.short_title: Brake Brothers v former buyers: enforcement of non-compete covenants
key_facts: Two national food buyers resigned from Brake Brothers after garden leave and intended to join rival wholesaler 3663.
Their contracts contained six-month post-termination restraints including non-compete, non-solicitation, confidentiality and non-enticement covenants.
Brakes argued the buyers had access to confidential trading agreement terms, business planning information and supplier connections akin to trade secrets.
3663 offered limited product-range undertakings and would pay the employees during any restraint period.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of an action for permanent injunctions to enforce post-termination restrictive covenants after interim relief was granted.
enrichment.outcome: Claim upheld; permanent injunctions granted in the terms sought restraining the defendants from competing with major rivals for six months after garden leave.
enrichment.ratio: A non-competition covenant may be reasonable where confidential information akin to trade secrets is difficult to police and may be carried in the employee's head; six months after three months' garden leave was not excessive to protect supplier connections, staff stability and confidential buying information in the annual trading cycle.
legal_issues: Whether Brakes had legitimate interests warranting an area covenant
Whether the non-compete clause was wider or longer than reasonably necessary
Whether confidential trading and business planning information was adequately particularised
Whether the court should refuse injunctive relief despite validity of the covenants
linked_authorities: Herbert Morris Ltd v Saxelby [1916] 1 AC 688
Faccenda Chicken Ltd v Fowler [1987] 1 Ch 117
Littlewoods Organisation Ltd v Harris [1997] 1 WLR 1472

notes: Planning judicial review; predetermination/bias ground succeeded on 4-3 committee vote.

enrichment.short_title: Ghadami v Harlow: planning permission quashed for committee chairman bias
key_facts: Harlow District Council granted planning permission for major redevelopment of the Harvey Centre town centre retail scheme.
Claimant Mohammed Ghadami owned commercial premises affected by the development and challenged the decision by judicial review.
Three members of the Planning Committee gave witness evidence supporting the challenge.
The committee resolved 4-3 to grant permission; the chairman, Councillor Garnett, was found to have shown apparent bias or predetermination.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a screening opinion and of a planning committee resolution granting planning permission.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused on the screening opinion challenge; permission granted on the planning permission challenge and, on substantive hearing, all grounds failed except apparent bias/predetermination, so the planning permission was quashed.
enrichment.ratio: Where a planning committee chairman demonstrated apparent bias or predetermination and the permission decision was passed by a bare 4-3 majority, his participation vitiates the decision and the grant of planning permission must be quashed.
legal_issues: Lawfulness of the EIA screening opinion
Compliance with development plan and PPG 6
Whether the committee chairman was apparently biased or had predetermined the application
Whether other procedural and merits grounds invalidated the permission

notes: Landmark ANH/GMC guidance judicial review; Munby J granted tailored declarations.

enrichment.short_title: Burke v GMC: lawfulness of guidance on withholding artificial nutrition
key_facts: Oliver Burke suffered from cerebellar ataxia and sought clarification about future provision of artificial nutrition and hydration (ANH).
He challenged GMC guidance entitled 'Withholding and Withdrawing Life-prolonging Treatment' as incompatible with his autonomy and Convention rights.
The claimant contended a competent patient's decision for ANH is determinative and that withdrawal before imminent death requires strong justification and often court involvement.
The GMC argued doctors must decide treatment in the patient's best interests where the patient lacks capacity.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review claim for declarations as to the lawfulness of GMC guidance on withholding and withdrawing life-prolonging treatment.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded in principle; declarations made that competent or valid advance decisions for ANH are determinative of best interests in relevant circumstances and that specified paragraphs of the GMC guidance were unlawful.
enrichment.ratio: A competent patient's decision that ANH should be provided is determinative of best interests at least where death is not imminent and the patient is not comatose; doctors who cannot comply must transfer care, and GMC guidance must reflect the heavy presumption in favour of life-prolonging treatment and the need for prior judicial authorisation in certain withdrawal cases.
legal_issues: Whether ANH constitutes medical treatment for best interests analysis
Extent of a competent patient's autonomy over life-prolonging treatment
Compatibility of GMC guidance with Articles 2, 3, 6, 8 and 14 ECHR
When court authorisation is required before withdrawing ANH
linked_authorities: Airedale NHS Trust v Bland [1993] AC 789
Re J (Adoption: Non-Patrial) [1998] INLR 424

notes: Licence hostel condition challenge partly succeeded on flawed OASys risk assessment.

enrichment.short_title: Carman: challenge to licence condition requiring probation hostel residence

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Court Services Act 2000

key_facts: Dr Carman, a former GP convicted of indecent assaults on patients, was released on licence after serving an 18-month sentence.
Licence conditions initially required residence at Brigstocke Road probation hostel with intensive reporting and excluded return to Weston-super-Mare.
He challenged the hostel requirement as irrational and contrary to Article 8, citing vulnerability due to a serious arm injury and flawed victim consultation.
Interim relief allowed him to live with a friend in Bristol while proceedings continued.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review, with leave, of licence conditions imposed on release from custody.
enrichment.outcome: Most grounds failed, but the hostel residence condition was quashed because the OASys risk assessment was flawed by proceeding on more convictions than remained after the Court of Appeal; risk must be reassessed promptly.
enrichment.ratio: Courts should rarely interfere with licence conditions based on probation risk assessment, but a written OASys assessment that materially overstates the offender's proven offending undermines the medium/high risk classification and vitiates a licence condition founded on that assessment.
legal_issues: Whether licence hostel residence infringed Article 8
Whether section 69 victim consultation requirements were breached
Whether two-hour reporting on hostel entry was irrational
Whether the OASys risk assessment was flawed after convictions were quashed
linked_authorities: Craven (R on the application of) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2001] EWHC Admin 850

confidence.notes: Outcome limited to quashing the hostel condition pending reassessment; court emphasised exceptional intervention standard.

notes: Article 8 family life in Indian adoption entry clearance case; Court of Appeal restored adjudicator.

enrichment.short_title: Singh v Entry Clearance Officer: family life and foreign adoption
key_facts: Pawandeep Singh, an Indian child, was adopted under Sikh custom and Indian law by UK-settled relatives after they could not have further children.
The adoption was valid in India but not recognised in UK immigration rules; entry clearance to join the sponsors was refused.
The sponsors visited regularly, financed and made major decisions for the child, who was raised to regard them as his real parents.
The adjudicator found Article 8 family life and a breach; the Immigration Appeal Tribunal held family life had not been established.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Immigration Appeal Tribunal on whether family life existed under Article 8 ECHR for an Indian adoption not recognised by UK law.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the adjudicator was entitled to find family life existed and the tribunal erred in overturning that decision.
enrichment.ratio: Whether Article 8 family life exists is a question of fact depending on close personal ties in practice; a lawful non-sham adoption valid in the child's home country may contribute to family life even if not recognised domestically, and failure to meet international adoption standards does not automatically negate family life.
legal_issues: Whether family life was established between the child and UK adoptive parents
Relevance of a valid Indian adoption not recognised by UK law
Application of Strasbourg jurisprudence including Pini and X and Y v UK
Whether the tribunal erred in requiring a stronger psychological bond
linked_authorities: Pini v Romania (ECtHR, 22 June 2004)
X and Y v United Kingdom (1978) 12 DR 32
Re J (Adoption: Non-Patrial) [1998] INLR 424

notes: Lloyd's premium debt summary judgment; residual defences held unarguable.

enrichment.short_title: Lloyd's v Levy and Johnson: summary judgment on Equitas premium debts
key_facts: Lloyd's sued Names Dr and Mrs Levy and Mr and Mrs Johnson for unpaid Equitas reinsurance premiums assigned under the 1996 Reconstruction and Renewal Plan.
The debts exceeded £300,000 for the Levys and over £500,000 for the Johnsons, plus interest.
Defendants sought to amend defences raising EU Directive 73/239, stamp duty, company charge registration and quantum points after extensive prior Lloyd's litigation.
Both defendant couples had participated in Jaffray and Laws actions but now pursued fresh arguments through new solicitors.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Combined Commercial Court applications for summary judgment and for permission to amend defences and counterclaims.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to amend refused on all proposed grounds; summary judgment granted for Lloyd's on the premium debt claims.
enrichment.ratio: Directive 73/239 did not confer directly effective rights on Lloyd's Names to challenge regulatory supervision; stamp duty and section 396 registration points were unarguable or already decided, and Equitas premium records were conclusive absent manifest error.
legal_issues: Direct effect of Directive 73/239 for Names challenging Lloyd's regulation
Whether assignment documents were inadmissible for want of stamp duty
Whether an unregistered charge under section 396 voided the debt against solvent Names
Whether proposed amendments were an abuse of process after Laws litigation

notes: Section 173(11) deemed permission appeal; Scott v SoS construction applied to dismiss appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Maldon v Hammond: section 173(11) and vehicle storage on rural land
key_facts: Mr Hammond used 5.2 acres at Mill Road, Mayland for car repair, storage of wrecked vehicles and habitation in a mobile home after his unlawfully built bungalow was demolished.
Maldon District Council obtained mandatory injunctions requiring removal of vehicles, structures and cessation of habitation use.
Mr Hammond argued that earlier 1997 enforcement notices, complied with in 2000, conferred deemed planning permission under section 173(11) for car-related uses not required to cease.
The judge found no ten-year change-of-use immunity and rejected the section 173(11) argument; Sedley LJ granted permission on the deemed-permission point only.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from mandatory planning injunctions after trial before Buckley J.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; section 173(11) did not grant deemed permission for vehicle storage because the enforcement notice did not allege that use as a breach of planning control; stay lifted.
enrichment.ratio: Section 173(11) applies only where an enforcement notice could have required cessation of a use that it alleges to be a breach of planning control; it does not deem permission for uses the authority did not identify as unlawful, following Scott v Secretary of State.
legal_issues: Whether car storage and repair amounted to a material change of use immune after ten years
Whether section 173(11) deemed planning permission for vehicle-related uses after compliance with 1997 notices
Whether the council could have amended enforcement notices to require cessation of car repair activity
Construction of ODPM Circular 10/97 guidance on under-enforcement
linked_authorities: Scott v Secretary of State for the Environment, Transport and the Regions [2000] CAT 16 October 1990
Fidler v First Secretary of State [2003] EWHC 2003 (Admin)
Tandridge District Council v Verrequia [2000] 1 QB 318

notes: Article 81 margin-squeeze appeal; Bayer unilateral conduct analysis upheld on summary judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Unipart v O2: Article 81 and unilateral margin squeeze on wholesale airtime
key_facts: Unipart, as an independent mobile service provider, bought wholesale airtime from O2 (formerly Cellnet) under standard facultative agreements allowing Cellnet to set published prices.
Unipart alleged Cellnet operated an anti-competitive margin squeeze cross-subsidising tied service providers between 1996 and 1999, breaching Article 81.
Cellnet applied for summary judgment contending margin squeeze was unilateral conduct, not an agreement between undertakings.
Lloyd J granted summary judgment for Cellnet; Unipart appealed, relying on Distillers and arguing agreement to pay prices sufficed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from summary judgment striking out Unipart's Article 81 damages claim against O2.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; agreeing to pay prices set unilaterally in standard terms did not constitute an Article 81 agreement to a margin-squeeze policy.
enrichment.ratio: Article 81 requires a concurrence of wills on the anti-competitive conduct complained of; a dealer's contractual agreement to pay a supplier's unilaterally set prices is not acquiescence in an underlying margin-squeeze policy, following Bayer AG v Commission.
legal_issues: Whether Unipart's airtime supply agreements were agreements between undertakings for Article 81 purposes
Whether tacit acquiescence in Cellnet's margin squeeze could be inferred from paying published prices
Distinction between Article 81 agreements and unilateral conduct addressable under Article 82
Whether the pleaded conduct restricted or distorted competition
linked_authorities: Bayer AG v European Commission (CFI) Case T-41/96
Bayer AG v European Commission (ECJ) Case C-2/01 P
Richard Cound Ltd v BMW (GB) Ltd [1997] EuLR 277
